summary: Defines a new chunk type, several parameters, and procedures for SCTP so that chunks can be authenticated using shared keys between sender and receiver. The new parameters help establish those keys. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A receiver wants proof that each piece of a message really came from the sender. This note adds a secret stamp to each piece.

questions: how does the sctp auth chunk work
what is the sctp hmac-algo parameter
which hash algorithms does sctp auth support
subtitle: A way for SCTP endpoints to prove that chunks really came from their peer, using an HMAC and shared keys.

tldr.problem: SCTP verification tags only guard against blind attackers, and TLS over SCTP secures only user data, so there was no way to prove that a chunk was sent by the peer that started the association.
tldr.mechanism: A new AUTH chunk carries an HMAC computed over the chunks that follow it. Endpoints agree on the hash algorithm and a per-association shared key through three new INIT parameters: RANDOM, CHUNKS and HMAC-ALGO.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can require selected chunk types to arrive authenticated and silently drop them otherwise. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted.

today: RFC 4895 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the SCTP specification in RFC 2960.

sections.title: Why SCTP Needs Authenticated Chunks
sections.content:
SCTP uses 32-bit verification tags to protect itself against blind attackers, and these values do not change during the life of an association. New SCTP extensions need a stronger tool: a way to prove that a chunk was sent by the original peer and not by a malicious attacker.

Using TLS as defined in RFC 3436 does not help, because it only secures SCTP user data. So RFC 4895 defines an extension that derives shared keys for each association. These association shared keys come from optional, configured endpoint pair shared keys (which might be empty) and from data exchanged during association setup.

The RFC also notes that the SCTP extension for Dynamic Address Reconfiguration (ADD-IP) requires this extension, and that the Partial Reliability Extension (PR-SCTP) can be used with it.
sections.eli5: Imagine a club where anyone can slip notes under the door. This idea gives members a secret handshake that goes with each note, so the club knows the note is really from a member.

sections.title: The Three New Parameters
sections.content:
Authentication is negotiated during association setup with three new parameters carried in the INIT or INIT-ACK chunk. Their types are 0x8002, 0x8003 and 0x8004. The upper bits of the type tell a receiver that does not understand them to ignore them and carry on.

  • RANDOM (0x8002) carries a random number. An endpoint that wants to send or receive authenticated chunks MUST include it once, with a 32-byte number.
  • CHUNKS (0x8003) lists the chunk types the sender requires to arrive authenticated. Its maximum length is 260 bytes. INIT, INIT-ACK, SHUTDOWN-COMPLETE and AUTH MUST NOT be listed.
  • HMAC-ALGO (0x8004) lists the HMAC identifiers the peer is asked to use, most preferred first. It MUST be included once if the sender wants to send or receive authenticated chunks.

Each parameter is padded with zero bytes to a 32-bit boundary, and receivers ignore the padding. The only HMAC that every endpoint MUST support is the one based on SHA-1.
sections.eli5: When two computers first meet, each says: here is a random number, here are the kinds of messages I want stamped, and here are the stamp styles I like.

sections.title: The AUTH Chunk and Error Cause
sections.content:
The new AUTH chunk has type 0x0F and holds the result of the HMAC calculation. Its fields are a flags byte (SHOULD be zero on transmit, ignored on receipt), a length, a 2-byte Shared Key Identifier saying which endpoint pair shared key is used, a 2-byte HMAC Identifier and the HMAC itself. The chunk length is the HMAC length plus 8, padded to a 32-bit boundary.

An AUTH chunk MUST NOT appear more than once in a packet. Every control and data chunk placed after it is authenticated; chunks placed before it are not.

The RFC puts the HMAC before the data it covers for two reasons. Putting it at the end would require a control chunk after DATA chunks, which breaks the rule that control chunks come first. It would also prevent sending the packet while the HMAC is being computed, because the HMAC is needed for the CRC32C checksum in the common header.

A new error cause, Unsupported HMAC Identifier (code 0x0105, length 6), reports an AUTH chunk that used an HMAC identifier the receiver does not support.
sections.eli5: The stamp is placed at the front of a bundle of notes and covers everything behind it. Anything in front of the stamp is not covered.

sections.title: Building the Association Shared Key
sections.content:
Both endpoints MAY hold endpoint pair shared keys, which are byte vectors that are pre-configured or set up by another mechanism and identified by the Shared Key Identifier. If there is none, an empty byte vector is used and one association shared key is computed.

Each endpoint concatenates the RANDOM, CHUNKS and HMAC-ALGO parameters it sent (type, length and value, with padding removed) into a key vector. The association shared key is the endpoint pair shared key, followed by the numerically smaller key vector, followed by the larger one. Comparisons use network byte order. If the vectors are equal as numbers but differ in length, the shorter goes first, and identical vectors can go in any order.

If the Random Number is not 32 bytes, the association MUST be aborted. The number should be generated as described in RFC 4086, and INIT collisions follow the same pattern as for the Verification Tag.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix their own secret numbers together in the same agreed order, so they end up with the same secret key without ever sending it.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Authenticated Chunks
sections.content:
A sender MUST authenticate every chunk the peer asked for, and MAY authenticate others. To do so it bundles those chunks after an AUTH chunk. With no endpoint pair shared key it MUST use Shared Key Identifier zero. It computes the HMAC (RFC 2104) over the AUTH chunk with its HMAC field set to zero, followed by all chunks after it, including their padding.

A receiver silently discards listed chunk types that arrive without a preceding AUTH chunk. It MUST use the HMAC algorithm named in the AUTH chunk; if that algorithm was not in its own HMAC-ALGO parameter, the AUTH chunk and the chunks after it are discarded and an ERROR chunk SHOULD be sent with the new error cause. If the shared key identifier is unknown, the authenticated chunks are silently discarded. If the recomputed HMAC does not match, the chunks after the AUTH chunk MUST be silently discarded.

COOKIE-ECHO needs special handling because it can create an association. If a packet starts with AUTH then COOKIE-ECHO and the receiver has no state for it, authentication is based on the parameters in the cookie. The cookie MUST NOT contain any endpoint pair shared keys.
sections.eli5: The sender puts the stamp on a bundle. The receiver redoes the stamp on its own and only opens the bundle if the two stamps match.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The simplest exchange sends INIT with RANDOM, CHUNKS and HMAC-ALGO, gets INIT-ACK with the same parameters, then continues with COOKIE-ECHO and COOKIE-ACK. The CHUNKS parameter is optional.

If the server wants DATA chunks authenticated, the client sends COOKIE-ECHO, AUTH and DATA together, and the server replies with COOKIE-ACK and SACK. When the endpoint pair shared key depends on the client and is known only to the upper layer, the server may need upper layer intervention between handling COOKIE-ECHO and handling AUTH and DATA. If the API makes that impossible, the server might discard AUTH and DATA, forcing a retransmission.
sections.eli5: Setting up is a short chat. If the server wants the very first message stamped, the client sends it in the same bundle as its reply.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without endpoint pair shared keys, the extension only protects against attackers who did not capture the initial handshake. With such a key, even a true man in the middle cannot inject chunks that must be authenticated, even after intercepting the handshake. Setting up endpoint pair shared keys is out of scope; TLS or manual configuration are given as options.

There is no built-in replay protection beyond SCTP's handling of duplicated chunks within an association. A separate association shared key per association covers replays across associations.

Requiring ABORT and COOKIE-ECHO to be authenticated stops an attacker from bringing down or restarting an association without the key. The cost is that dead peers may take longer to detect and the restart procedure fails unless the restarting endpoint knows the old key.

An endpoint that lists several HMAC algorithms must be ready for the peer to use the weakest. If non-NULL keys are in use but an endpoint still accepts a NULL key, an attacker who captured the handshake can still inject or modify authenticated chunks.
sections.eli5: A shared secret keeps strangers out. But if you also let people in with no password, or accept the weakest stamp, the lock is only as good as that weak spot.

items.label: SHA-1
items.desc: Every endpoint supporting chunk authentication MUST support it.
